whyWrongByChoice.C: Malignant melanoma is not among the malignancies associated with CVID in this source.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic myeloid leukemia is not the malignancy CVID patients are noted to be at risk for.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepatocellular carcinoma is not described as a CVID-associated cancer here.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy has eczema and recurrent bacterial and viral infections, and Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is suspected. Which of the following laboratory findings is required to make this diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Small platelets with a count below 70,000/microliter

choices.label: C
choices.text: Absent CD40 ligand on activated T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: An isolated low serum IgA with normal IgG

choices.label: E
choices.text: Elevated serum IgM with low IgG and IgA

explanation.summary: Diagnosing WAS requires demonstrating small and few platelets (below 70,000/microliter) plus a confirmatory genetic or protein finding.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagnosis of WAS requires the presence of small and few platelets (below 70,000/microliter) along with one of the following: a WAS mutation, absent WAS protein, absent WAS mRNA by Northern blot, or affected male maternal relatives with few, small platelets. The small, low platelet count is the required hallmark.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Serum IgE above 1,000 IU/mL confirms hyper-IgE syndrome, not Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Absent CD40L on T cells is a confirmatory test for X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An isolated low IgA with normal IgG defines selective IgA deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Elevated IgM with low IgG and IgA is the pattern of X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome, not WAS.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with recurrent nontuberculous mycobacterial infections is diagnosed with MSMD caused by an IL-12 receptor beta-1 mutation; testing shows his interferon-gamma receptor is intact. In addition to aggressive antimycobacterial antibiotics, which of the following therapies is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: MSMD is treated with aggressive antimycobacterials, and IFN-gamma therapy is used when the IFN-gamma receptor is intact.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with active MSMD infections receive aggressive treatment with antimycobacterial antibiotics. Interferon-gamma therapy is appropriate when the IFN-gamma receptor is intact, as in this child whose defect is upstream at the IL-12 receptor, so supplying IFN-gamma can still activate downstream signaling; HSCT is another option in some cases.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunoglobulin replacement is used for antibody deficiencies such as CVID and X-HIMS, but MSMD patients have normal immunoglobulin levels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelet transfusion is part of managing Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, not MSMD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Belimumab is an anti-BAFF biologic used in SLE, not a treatment for MSMD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgA-deficient blood products are a precaution for selective IgA deficiency during transfusion, unrelated to MSMD therapy.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman undergoing evaluation for mild recurrent sinusitis is found to have a low serum IgA with normal IgG, IgM, and IgE. Her physician explains that she has the most common adaptive inborn error of immunity. Which of the following best describes the incidence of this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: As high as 1:100, depending on the population

explanation.summary: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common adaptive IEI, with an incidence as high as 1:100.
explanation.whyCorrect: Selective Ig deficiencies are a class of humoral immunodeficiency in which only a single Ig isotype is deficient. Selective IgA deficiency is the most common of that class and the most common adaptive IEI overall, with an incidence as high as 1:100 depending on the population studied.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An incidence of 1:25,000 in adults describes CVID, the second most common IEI in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An incidence of 1:100,000 live births describes Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An incidence of 1:1,000,000 describes hyper-IgM syndrome, a rare disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Selective IgA deficiency is far more common than 1:1,000; the figure cited is up to 1:100.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has had recurrent otitis media, sinusitis, and several episodes of gastroenteritis over the past 2 years but no skin abscesses, bleeding, or deep-seated infections. Serum studies show an undetectable IgA with normal IgG, IgM, and IgE, and B and T cell counts are normal. Which of the following best explains why her infections cluster at these particular sites?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgA is the dominant antibody class protecting respiratory and GI mucosal epithelia

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgA is the principal opsonin for encapsulated bacteria in the bloodstream

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgA is required to activate the classical complement pathway on pathogens

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgA is the antibody class transferred across the placenta to protect infants

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgA is needed to recruit neutrophils to sites of extracellular infection

explanation.summary: IgA is the dominant antibody in mucosal secretions, so its deficiency manifests as ear, sinus, and GI infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: IgA is the dominant antibody class in mucosal secretions and plays an important role in protecting the GI, respiratory, and urogenital mucosal epithelia. When selective IgA deficiency is symptomatic, it therefore presents as recurrent ear, sinus, and gastrointestinal infections rather than systemic or deep infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Opsonization of encapsulated bacteria in blood is not the role attributed to IgA; IgA acts at mucosal surfaces.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Classical complement activation is not described as an IgA function and would not explain a mucosal infection pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The antibody that crosses the placenta is IgG, which is why X-HIMS infants can have normal IgG initially.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophil recruitment to extracellular infections is the role of Th17 cells and IL-17, not IgA.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man with selective IgA deficiency diagnosed 3 years ago has remained entirely asymptomatic and asks whether he still needs follow-up visits. Which of the following is the best reason to continue monitoring him?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A small percentage of patients go on to lose additional classes of antibodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most patients eventually develop non-Hodgkin lymphoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most patients eventually develop disseminated mycobacterial disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgA levels usually normalize, at which point precautions can be dropped

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neutropenia develops in the majority of patients over time

explanation.summary: Patients with selective IgA deficiency need monitoring because some progress to lose other antibody classes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although most patients with selective IgA deficiency are asymptomatic and need no treatment, they should be closely monitored. By a mechanism that is unknown, a small percentage will go on to lose additional classes of antibodies, which would change both the diagnosis and the management.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a feature of CVID, and even there it is a risk, not the fate of most patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Disseminated mycobacterial disease is the hallmark of MSMD, not a complication of selective IgA deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick does not describe IgA levels normalizing; the concern is progression to broader antibody loss, not resolution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutropenia in the majority of patients is a feature of X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome (65%), not selective IgA deficiency.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A previously well 67-year-old man with anemia and low vitamin B12 receives a red cell transfusion for exertional dyspnea. Ten minutes into the transfusion he feels unwell and sweaty; at 60 minutes he has a temperature of 38.2 C, a systolic blood pressure that has fallen from 140 to 90 mm Hg, and a widespread urticarial rash without lip swelling or wheeze. Subsequent testing shows an undetectable serum IgA with normal IgG and IgM. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgE specific for IgA triggered a type I hypersensitivity response to donor IgA

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgM against donor red cell antigens activated complement on the transfused cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune complexes of donor plasma proteins deposited in small vessels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sensitized T cells reacted against donor leukocytes in a delayed response

choices.label: E
choices.text: Anti-IgA antibodies opsonized the patient's own B cells for destruction

explanation.summary: In selective IgA deficiency, prior sensitization produces anti-IgA IgE, and donor IgA then triggers type I anaphylaxis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because this patient does not produce IgA, he never developed tolerance to it. At some earlier point he was exposed to IgA and became sensitized, developing IgG and IgE specific for IgA. On re-exposure to IgA in the donor blood, an IgE-mediated transfusion reaction occurred immediately through a type I hypersensitivity response. The anaphylaxis must be treated immediately, and future transfusions should use IgA-deficient or washed blood products.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement-mediated lysis of donor red cells is not the mechanism described; the reaction is directed at IgA in the donor product, not red cell antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune complex deposition is a type III mechanism, whereas the transfusion reaction in IgA deficiency is an immediate IgE-mediated type I response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A T cell-mediated response would be delayed, not evident within 10 to 60 minutes with urticaria and hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The anti-IgA antibodies target IgA in the transfused product, not the patient's own B cells.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy with selective IgA deficiency has had six episodes of sinusitis and three of otitis media in the past year, two requiring hospitalization. His IgG, IgM, and IgE remain normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

explanation.summary: Selective IgA deficiency with severe, recurrent infections is managed with prophylactic antibiotics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with selective IgA deficiency usually require no treatment, but those with severe, recurrent infections may benefit from prophylactic antibiotics. This boy has frequent sinopulmonary infections requiring hospitalization, so antibiotic prophylaxis is the appropriate escalation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunoglobulin replacement is used for CVID, X-HIMS, and WAS; his IgG is normal, and IgA is not replaced this way.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon-gamma therapy is used in MSMD when the IFN-gamma receptor is intact, not for IgA deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HSCT is reserved for severe conditions such as WAS or severe X-HIMS, not selective IgA deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: G-CSF treats the neutropenia of X-HIMS; there is no neutropenia here.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with recurrent sinopulmonary infections has low IgG and IgA with normal B and T cell counts. Genetic testing identifies a loss-of-function mutation in the gene encoding inducible co-stimulator (ICOS). Loss of which of the following normal functions best accounts for her hypogammaglobulinemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stabilizing follicular helper T cell-B cell binding and boosting CD40L expression

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delivering the BAFF survival signal that maintains B cell homeostasis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transcytosing secretory IgA across the mucosal epithelium into the lumen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Driving naive T cells to differentiate into IL-17-secreting Th17 cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Activating actin polymerization within hematopoietic cells

explanation.summary: ICOS on follicular helper T cells binds ICOSL on B cells to stabilize the interaction and increase CD40L expression.
explanation.whyCorrect: ICOS-ICOSL is one of two commonly affected receptor-ligand pairs in CVID. The binding of ICOS on follicular helper T cells to ICOSL on B cells stabilizes the T cell-B cell interaction and promotes increased expression of CD40L. Losing this support impairs the plasma cell production that underlies the loss of IgG plus IgA and/or IgM in CVID.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The B cell survival signal is delivered by BAFF through its receptors (such as TACI), a separate CVID-associated pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transcytosis of secretory IgA is the function of the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor, relevant to IgA deficiency redundancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Th17 differentiation depends on STAT3; its loss causes hyper-IgE syndrome, not CVID.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Actin polymerization in hematopoietic cells depends on WASP, the protein lost in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man is diagnosed with common variable immunodeficiency after presenting with recurrent pneumonia and autoimmune hemolytic anemia. A gene panel is ordered. A mutation affecting which of the following is the most common genetic association with his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A receptor for B cell activating factor (TACI)

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD40 ligand on activated T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The beta chain of the IL-12 receptor

explanation.summary: Mutations in a BAFF receptor (TACI, also called CVID) are the most common genetic association with CVID.
explanation.whyCorrect: B cell activating factor (BAFF) is a B cell survival factor critical for B cell homeostasis and function. Mutations in one of the BAFF receptors are the most common genetic association with CVID, so much so that one of the names for this receptor is CVID; immunologists call it TACI. Multiple mutations in multiple pathways can produce the phenotype, but the BAFF receptor is the most common.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD40L mutations cause X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome, with high IgM rather than the broad hypogammaglobulinemia of CVID.
whyWrongByChoice.C: STAT3 defects cause hyper-IgE syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: WASP mutations cause Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-12 receptor beta chain mutations cause MSMD.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is started on belimumab. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Monoclonal antibody that binds and inhibits BAFF

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monoclonal antibody that blocks CD40L-CD40 binding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Growth factor that stimulates neutrophil production

explanation.summary: Belimumab is an anti-BAFF monoclonal antibody and was the first biologic licensed for SLE.
explanation.whyCorrect: BAFF, the B cell survival factor whose receptor mutations are linked to CVID, is commonly overexpressed in SLE and is strongly involved in the pathogenesis of the disease. Belimumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds and inhibits BAFF, and it was the first biologic agent licensed for SLE therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The PI3K-delta inhibitor is leniolisib, used for the PI3KCD gain-of-function form of CVID.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking CD40L-CD40 is not belimumab's mechanism; CD40L is the molecule lost in X-HIMS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recombinant interferon-gamma is a therapy for MSMD with an intact IFN-gamma receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A neutrophil growth factor describes G-CSF, used for the neutropenia of X-HIMS.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy with common variable immunodeficiency is maintained on immunoglobulin replacement. Genetic testing reveals a gain-of-function mutation in PI3KCD, which encodes a subunit of a kinase involved in B and T cell signal transduction. Which of the following targeted therapies is indicated for his form of the disease?

explanation.summary: PI3KCD gain-of-function CVID is treated with leniolisib, a PI3K-delta inhibitor.
explanation.whyCorrect: One form of CVID is due to a gain-of-function mutation in the PI3KCD gene, which encodes a subunit of PI3K, a kinase involved in B and T cell signal transduction. Because the mutation increases kinase activity, a PI3K-delta inhibitor, leniolisib, is indicated for the treatment of this form of CVID.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Belimumab inhibits BAFF and is used in SLE; it does not counter an overactive PI3K.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon-gamma is used in MSMD when the IFN-gamma receptor is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: G-CSF addresses the neutropenia of X-HIMS, not a kinase gain-of-function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gene therapy is described as a management option for Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, not for this form of CVID.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with common variable immunodeficiency has had three hospitalizations for pneumonia in the past year, and a chest CT now demonstrates bronchiectasis. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

explanation.summary: CVID with recurrent infections and bronchiectasis is treated with both immunoglobulin replacement and prophylactic antibiotics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Management of CVID is based on infection frequency and severity. Patients with recurrent infections and bronchiectasis are given both immunoglobulin replacement and prophylactic antibiotics. Chronic lung disease, especially bronchiectasis, affects 30% to 50% of patients and is an important cause of morbidity and mortality, so patients should also be monitored for bronchiectasis and lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelet transfusions are part of WAS management; CVID does not involve thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon-gamma with antimycobacterial antibiotics is the regimen for MSMD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: G-CSF is for the neutropenia of X-HIMS, and antifungal prophylaxis is emphasized in HIES, not CVID.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leniolisib is only for the PI3KCD gain-of-function form of CVID, and IgA-deficient blood products are a precaution in selective IgA deficiency.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with recurrent sinusitis and pneumonia and a recent diagnosis of autoimmune thyroiditis has a low serum IgG and low IgM with a normal IgA. Flow cytometry shows normal B and T cell counts. Before common variable immunodeficiency is diagnosed, which of the following is required?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exclusion of other causes of hypogammaglobulinemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Demonstration of absent CD40L on activated T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: A serum IgE greater than 1,000 IU/mL

choices.label: E
choices.text: Demonstration of absent B cells on flow cytometry

explanation.summary: CVID is a diagnosis that requires low IgG plus another low isotype and exclusion of other causes of hypogammaglobulinemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: CVID should be suspected in patients with recurrent infections, especially those with autoimmune disease. For diagnosis, IgG must be low in addition to another immunoglobulin class (typically IgM and/or IgA), and the diagnosis requires that other causes of hypogammaglobulinemia have been excluded. Gene panels and genome sequencing may aid the diagnosis, and most patients are diagnosed between ages 20 and 40.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Absent CD40L on T cells is the confirmatory finding for X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome, not CVID.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Small platelets below 70,000/microliter are a diagnostic requirement for Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An IgE above 1,000 IU/mL confirms hyper-IgE syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: B and T cell counts are commonly normal in CVID; absent B cells occur in only some patients and are not required.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 20-month-old boy with X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome has a markedly elevated serum IgM with undetectable IgG and IgA. His B cells are present in normal numbers and express surface IgM normally. The inability of his B cells to switch isotype is most directly the result of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of B cells to enter the germinal center after CD40 engagement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of B cells to receive the BAFF survival signal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of B cells to bind the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of B cells to differentiate under STAT3 signaling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of B cells to polymerize actin for immune synapse formation

explanation.summary: CD40L-CD40 binding lets B cells enter the germinal center, where class switching occurs; X-HIMS blocks this step.
explanation.whyCorrect: The binding of CD40L on T cells to CD40 on B cells allows B cells to enter the germinal center. In the germinal center reaction, B cells may class switch from IgM production to IgA, IgE, or IgG. In X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome the mutated CD40L prevents T cells from interacting with the B cell so that it can undergo class switching, leaving IgM high and the other isotypes absent.

whyWrongByChoice.B: BAFF is a survival and homeostasis factor for B cells; his B cell numbers are normal, and BAFF defects are linked to CVID.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The polymeric Ig receptor transcytoses secretory IgA and IgM across mucosa; it is not involved in class switching.
whyWrongByChoice.D: STAT3 drives naive T cells toward Th17; its loss causes hyper-IgE syndrome, not a class-switching block.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Actin polymerization depends on WASP and is defective in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, not X-HIMS.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-week-old boy is evaluated because a maternal uncle died in infancy of X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome. He is well. His serum IgG and IgM are within normal limits for age. His parents ask whether this excludes the diagnosis. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgG may be normal now because of transplacental maternal IgG that will wane

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgG is normal because he inherited his mother's unaffected X chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgG is normal because CD40L is not expressed on T cells until age 2 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgG is normal because IgM fully compensates for class switching in infancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgG is normal because neutropenia, not low IgG, defines the disease

explanation.summary: In X-HIMS, immunoglobulin levels may be normal initially because of transplacental IgG; only as it wanes does the high-IgM pattern emerge.
explanation.whyCorrect: In X-HIMS, Ig levels may be normal initially due to transplacental IgG, but as this maternal IgG wanes, only IgM is detected: the IgM level is high while IgG, IgE, and IgA become very low or absent. A normal IgG at 6 weeks therefore does not exclude the diagnosis, and the definitive evaluation includes CD40L expression on T cells and genetic testing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A normal IgG at this age cannot show which X chromosome he inherited, because the IgG is maternal in origin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nothing in the disease description delays CD40L expression to age 2; the age 2 figure is when patients typically present, not when CD40L appears.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgM does not substitute for IgG; the defining pattern of X-HIMS is high IgM with absent IgG, IgE, and IgA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutropenia is present in 65% of patients but does not define the disease; the immunoglobulin pattern and absent CD40L do.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome receives immunoglobulin replacement and prophylaxis against bacterial, fungal, and opportunistic infections. A complete blood count shows an absolute neutrophil count of 400/microliter. Which of the following should be added to his regimen?

explanation.summary: Neutropenia in X-HIMS is treated with G-CSF alongside Ig replacement and antimicrobial prophylaxis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutropenia is present in 65% of patients with X-HIMS. Management of X-HIMS includes prophylaxis against bacterial, fungal, and opportunistic infection, administration of G-CSF, and immunoglobulin replacement. G-CSF is the component that addresses the neutropenia this boy has developed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Interferon-gamma is a therapy for MSMD when the IFN-gamma receptor is intact; it does not treat neutropenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Belimumab inhibits BAFF and is used in SLE, not in X-HIMS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leniolisib is a PI3K-delta inhibitor for the PI3KCD gain-of-function form of CVID.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet transfusions are used in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome; his problem is low neutrophils, not platelets.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with severe X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome complicated by persistent severe neutropenia is referred for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation while he is clinically stable. Which of the following best explains why transplantation is recommended now rather than deferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HSCT should precede the liver disease and hematologic malignancies these patients are prone to

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transplacental maternal IgG will stop protecting him from infection after age 5 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Class switching can be restored only while germinal centers are still forming

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutropenia in this condition becomes irreversible once the child reaches school age

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immunoglobulin replacement induces anti-IgA antibodies with prolonged use

explanation.summary: In severe X-HIMS, HSCT is done early because these patients are at increased risk of liver disease and hematologic malignancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: With severe X-HIMS, or moderate X-HIMS complicated by severe neutropenia, HSCT should be considered. Because these patients have an increased risk of liver diseases and hematologic malignancies, HSCT should be done before these complications occur, which is why transplantation is pursued while the child is still stable.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Transplacental IgG wanes over the first months of life, not at age 5, and is not the reason for transplant timing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick gives no window in which germinal center function must be restored; the timing rationale is complication avoidance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The neutropenia of X-HIMS is managed with G-CSF; no age-dependent irreversibility is described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-IgA antibodies are a concern in selective IgA deficiency with blood products, not a consequence of Ig replacement in X-HIMS.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy has had recurrent pneumonia and 6 weeks of diarrhea. A maternal cousin had a similar illness in infancy. Serum studies show elevated IgM with very low IgG and IgA. Before attributing these findings to X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome, which of the following must be excluded?

explanation.summary: HIV infection must be ruled out before diagnosing X-HIMS.
explanation.whyCorrect: X-HIMS should be suspected in a male infant with a family history of immunodeficiency, but HIV infection needs to be ruled out first. Initial evaluation then involves a CBC with differential and quantification of B cells, T cells, and Ig levels, followed by lymphocyte stimulation assays and genetic testing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: SLE is mentioned in the context of BAFF overexpression and belimumab, not as a mimic of X-HIMS in infancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Selective IgA deficiency shows an isolated low IgA with normal IgG and IgM, which does not match his high IgM and low IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cystic fibrosis is not among the conditions the brick requires excluding for this diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron deficiency anemia would not produce an immunoglobulin pattern of high IgM with low IgG and IgA.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl has a history of recurrent skin abscesses that lack warmth or tenderness, chronic eczema, and two episodes of pneumonia. Her serum IgE is 2,800 IU/mL. Her mother and maternal grandfather had similar abscesses and eczema in childhood. Which of the following is the most likely pattern of inheritance?

explanation.summary: Hyper-IgE syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so a family history is typical.
explanation.whyCorrect: This girl has the classic HIES triad of cold abscesses, sinopulmonary infections, and eczema with an IgE above 1,000 IU/mL. HIES is a rare disorder that inherits in an autosomal dominant pattern from a STAT3 defect. Because it is autosomal dominant, a family history is typical in all but novel mutations, matching the affected mother and grandfather across generations.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal recessive inheritance describes IL12RB-mediated MSMD, not HIES, and would not produce affected parent and grandparent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: X-linked recessive inheritance describes X-HIMS and WAS, which affect males; this affected girl with an affected mother does not fit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIES is autosomal, not X-linked, in its inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mitochondrial inheritance is not the pattern described for any IEI in this brick.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with STAT3-deficient hyper-IgE syndrome has a serum IgE of 4,200 IU/mL and peripheral eosinophilia. Which of the following best explains his elevated IgE?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of the Th17 pathway leaves Th2 cells elevated, favoring class switching to IgE

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess CD40L on T cells drives B cells repeatedly through germinal centers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Overexpression of BAFF prolongs the survival of IgE-secreting plasma cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of IgA class switching diverts all mucosal B cells toward IgE

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unopposed IFN-gamma from Th1 cells directly induces IgE production

explanation.summary: Without STAT3-driven Th17 differentiation, Th2 cells are elevated and B cells are more likely to class switch to IgE.
explanation.whyCorrect: STAT3 is a transcription factor critical for the differentiation of naive T cells into Th17 cells. Without this route of differentiation, Th2 cells are elevated and B cells are more likely to class switch to IgE, producing the markedly elevated IgE and, in roughly 50% of patients, tissue and blood eosinophilia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD40L is not overexpressed in HIES; CD40L loss is the defect in X-HIMS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: BAFF overexpression is described in SLE, not as the cause of high IgE in HIES.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgA class switching is not the defect in HIES; impaired IgA switching is the proposed basis of selective IgA deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IFN-gamma promotes Th1 responses and macrophage activation; the brick attributes the IgE rise to an exaggerated Th2 response, not IFN-gamma.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy has cold abscesses, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and eczema, and hyper-IgE syndrome is suspected. Which of the following serum IgE results would confirm the diagnosis?

explanation.summary: HIES is confirmed by an IgE above 1,000 IU/mL (normal below 150 IU/mL) plus genetic testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagnosis of HIES is suspected with the classic triad and confirmed with elevated IgE greater than 1,000 IU/mL together with genetic testing; normal IgE is less than 150 IU/mL. Only 1,600 IU/mL exceeds the confirmatory threshold. Tissue and blood eosinophilia may also be present.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 90 IU/mL is within the normal range of less than 150 IU/mL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 140 IU/mL is still below the 150 IU/mL upper limit of normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 300 IU/mL is above normal but well below the greater-than-1,000 IU/mL level required for confirmation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 800 IU/mL is elevated but does not reach the greater-than-1,000 IU/mL confirmatory threshold.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with confirmed STAT3-deficient hyper-IgE syndrome is being discharged after treatment of a Staphylococcus aureus skin abscess. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prophylaxis against bacterial and fungal infections

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgA-deficient blood products for any transfusion

explanation.summary: Management of HIES is prophylaxis against bacterial and fungal infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: Management of hyper-IgE syndrome includes prophylaxis against bacterial and fungal infections. Because Th17 cells that recruit neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi are lost, prophylactic antibiotics and antifungals are the indicated long-term therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelet transfusions are for the thrombocytopenia of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome; platelets are not affected in HIES.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon-gamma therapy is used in MSMD with an intact IFN-gamma receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgA-deficient blood products are a precaution in selective IgA deficiency because of anaphylaxis risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leniolisib is a PI3K-delta inhibitor for the PI3KCD gain-of-function form of CVID.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome has prolonged bleeding after minor trauma and has had severe, prolonged viral infections. Although actin polymerization supports many immune processes, loss of WASP particularly inhibits which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytotoxic T cell and platelet function

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutrophil respiratory burst and complement fixation

choices.label: D
choices.text: B cell class switching and plasma cell survival

explanation.summary: WASP loss impairs many actin-dependent functions, but cytotoxic T cell and platelet functions are particularly inhibited.
explanation.whyCorrect: WASP is expressed exclusively in hematopoietic cells and is critical in the activation of actin polymerization. Actin filaments are the major constituent of the cytoskeleton responsible for cellular movement, so inhibiting polymerization affects many immune functions, but cytotoxic T cell and platelet functions are particularly inhibited. This explains the bleeding and the susceptibility to viral infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Respiratory burst is one of many actin-influenced neutrophil processes in the figure, but it is not singled out as particularly inhibited, and complement fixation is not described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Th17 differentiation and IL-17 secretion depend on STAT3 and are lost in hyper-IgE syndrome, not WAS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Class switching depends on CD40L-CD40 signaling and is the defect in X-HIMS; plasma cell survival relates to BAFF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Macrophage activation by IFN-gamma is the pathway lost in MSMD and, via CD40L, in X-HIMS.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: An 8-month-old boy with eczema and recurrent otitis media has a platelet count of 45,000/microliter with small platelets. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is suspected, and genetic testing is pending. Which of the following family history findings would, together with his platelet findings, satisfy the diagnostic criteria?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A maternal uncle with few, small platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: His father with few, small platelets

choices.label: C
choices.text: A paternal grandfather with few, small platelets

choices.label: D
choices.text: An older sister with severe eczema

choices.label: E
choices.text: His mother with recurrent otitis media

explanation.summary: WAS can be diagnosed with small, few platelets plus affected male relatives on the side of the X-chromosome-donating parent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diagnosis of WAS requires small and few platelets (below 70,000/microliter) plus one of the following: a WAS mutation, absent WAS protein, absent WAS mRNA by Northern blot, or male cousins, uncles, or nephews with few, small platelets on the side of the X-chromosome-donating parent. A boy receives his X chromosome from his mother, so a maternal uncle with few, small platelets satisfies this criterion.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A father does not donate his X chromosome to a son, so paternal thrombocytopenia cannot reflect the same X-linked WAS mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The paternal grandfather is on the side of the parent who did not donate the boy's X chromosome, so this does not meet the criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Eczema in a sister is not a platelet finding, and the criterion specifies male relatives with few, small platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recurrent otitis in the mother is not the platelet finding in a male relative that the criterion requires.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with MSMD due to an IFNGR1 mutation has recovered from disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex infection. His parents ask what other infections he is prone to. Besides mycobacteria, clinical disease caused by which of the following affects about half of patients with this condition?

explanation.summary: About half of MSMD patients suffer clinical disease from Salmonella or other intramacrophagic organisms.
explanation.whyCorrect: MSMD patients are susceptible to weakly virulent intracellular bacteria because Th1 responses and macrophage activation are lost. Beyond BCG, nontuberculous mycobacteria, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis, about half suffer from clinical disease caused by Salmonella species or other intramacrophagic bacteria (listeriosis, nocardiosis, klebsiellosis), fungi (candidiasis, histoplasmosis), or parasites (leishmaniasis, toxoplasmosis).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pneumocystis is an opportunistic infection associated with the macrophage activation defect of X-HIMS, not the organism the brick links to half of MSMD patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Staphylococcus aureus cold abscesses characterize hyper-IgE syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cryptosporidium diarrhea is associated with X-HIMS, not with MSMD in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Susceptibility to viral infections is emphasized in WAS and X-HIMS, whereas MSMD susceptibility centers on intramacrophagic organisms.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy develops disseminated BCG infection after vaccination and is found to have a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in IL12RB. His parents are first cousins and are both healthy, with no family history of mycobacterial disease. Which of the following statements about the inheritance of his condition is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IL12RB mutations tend to be autosomal recessive, unlike some dominant IFN-gamma receptor mutations

choices.label: B
choices.text: IL12RB mutations are X-linked, which is why affected patients are typically male

choices.label: C
choices.text: IL12RB mutations are autosomal dominant, so a family history is typical in all but novel mutations

choices.label: D
choices.text: IL12RB mutations are inherited identically to IFN-gamma receptor mutations, which are always recessive

choices.label: E
choices.text: IL12RB mutations arise sporadically and show no familial clustering

explanation.summary: IL12RB mutations are autosomal recessive, while IFN-gamma receptor mutations are autosomal variable (mostly recessive, some dominant).
explanation.whyCorrect: MSMD can be caused by over 20 loss-of-function mutations along the Th1 differentiation and activation pathway. Two critical types are mutations in the beta chain of the IL-12 receptor (IL12RB) and in the IFN-gamma receptors (IFNGR1 or IFNGR2). IL12RB mutations tend to inherit in an autosomal recessive pattern, consistent with healthy consanguineous parents, whereas IFN-gamma receptor mutations are autosomal variable, most recessive but one or more dominant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IL12RB mutations are autosomal, not X-linked; X-linked inheritance describes X-HIMS and WAS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autosomal dominant inheritance with a typical family history describes hyper-IgE syndrome, not IL12RB-mediated MSMD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IFN-gamma receptor mutations are not always recessive; one or more are dominant, so the two are not inherited identically.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The autosomal recessive pattern of IL12RB mutations is a familial pattern, not sporadic occurrence.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Adaptive Immunity (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated in clinic because she feels she gets sick "more than everyone else." Which of the following aspects of her history would most strongly prompt an evaluation for an underlying immunodeficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One episode of community-acquired pneumonia three years ago

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two episodes of pneumonia within the past 12 months

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single uncomplicated urinary tract infection last winter

choices.label: E
choices.text: One episode of streptococcal pharyngitis two years ago

explanation.summary: Recurrent infections that meet frequency thresholds, such as two or more pneumonias in a year, are a hallmark warning sign of immunodeficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists recurrent infections as a warning sign, defined by high frequency such as at least 4 confirmed bacterial infections per year, at least 2 pneumonias per year, or at least 4 new ear infections in a year. Two documented pneumonias in a single year meets this threshold and warrants an immunodeficiency evaluation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single, remote episode of pneumonia is not recurrent and does not meet the frequency threshold that raises concern for immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: One uncomplicated urinary tract infection is common in the general population and is not among the recurrent, severe, unusual, or persistent warning signs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Allergic rhinitis reflects atopy, not an increased susceptibility to serious or opportunistic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An isolated episode of streptococcal pharyngitis is a routine infection and does not indicate an underlying immune defect.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man has had three episodes of pneumonia over two years, each localized to the right middle lobe. His immunoglobulin levels, lymphocyte subsets, and complement studies are all normal. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his recurrent infections?

explanation.summary: Recurrent infection confined to a single anatomic area is more likely due to a local anatomic defect than to a systemic immunodeficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that infection in a single anatomic area is more likely due to a congenital or acquired anatomic abnormality (such as right middle lobe pneumonia from anatomic obstruction) than to immunodeficiency. His normal immune labs further argue against a systemic immune defect.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Common variable immunodeficiency causes hypogammaglobulinemia and infections at multiple sites; his immunoglobulin levels are normal and disease is localized.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Late complement deficiencies predispose to recurrent Neisseria infections, not repeated same-lobe pneumonia, and his complement studies are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic granulomatous disease causes recurrent abscesses with catalase-positive organisms across many sites, not isolated single-lobe pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked agammaglobulinemia presents in early childhood with absent B cells and very low immunoglobulins, inconsistent with this adult and his normal labs.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnea and a dry cough. Chest imaging shows diffuse interstitial infiltrates, and bronchoalveolar lavage confirms Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. A deficiency in which of the following is most likely responsible for this infection?

explanation.summary: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is an opportunistic infection that reflects decreased T-cell (cell-mediated) function.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia as an opportunistic infection seen with low CD4 counts in HIV, and its review question specifies that this infection is most suggestive of decreased T-cell function. Recurrent opportunistic infection points to a cell-mediated immune defect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement deficiencies predispose to recurrent Neisseria infection, not Pneumocystis pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A defective neutrophil oxidative burst (as in CGD) causes catalase-positive bacterial and fungal abscesses, not Pneumocystis pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Asplenia predisposes to overwhelming encapsulated bacterial infection, not to Pneumocystis, which is an opportunist controlled by T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Selective IgA deficiency predisposes to mucosal and sinopulmonary bacterial infections, not to opportunistic Pneumocystis pneumonia.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student is admitted with his second episode of Neisseria meningitidis meningitis in two years. Which of the following laboratory studies is most likely to reveal his underlying immune defect?

explanation.summary: Recurrent Neisseria infection points to a complement deficiency, which is evaluated with CH50, AH50, C3, and C4.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's evaluation schema lists recurrent or severe Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Neisseria meningitidis infection as the trigger to test complement, with a diagnostic workup of CH50, AH50, C3, and C4. Late (MAC) complement deficiencies specifically predispose to Neisseria infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immunoglobulin levels evaluate humoral defects, which typically cause encapsulated bacterial and sinopulmonary infections rather than recurrent Neisseria meningitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The oxidative burst assay screens for phagocytic defects such as CGD, which cause catalase-positive abscesses, not recurrent Neisseria disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV is worth screening broadly, but recurrent Neisseria meningitis specifically implicates the complement pathway rather than CD4 T-cell loss.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin A1c screens for diabetes; hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil function but is not the classic cause of recurrent Neisseria meningitis.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent skin and liver abscesses caused by catalase-positive bacteria and fungi, including Serratia and Aspergillus. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

explanation.summary: Recurrent abscesses from catalase-positive organisms suggest a phagocytic defect, evaluated with the neutrophil oxidative burst assay.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pediatric evaluation schema directs that recurrent infection with catalase-positive bacteria and fungi, or abscesses and osteomyelitis, should raise suspicion for a phagocytic defect such as chronic granulomatous disease. The diagnostic evaluation includes the neutrophil oxidative burst assay and peripheral blood smear.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunoglobulin levels evaluate humoral defects, which present with encapsulated bacterial infections rather than catalase-positive abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complement assays are indicated for recurrent Neisseria infection, not for catalase-positive abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Post-vaccination antibody titers assess humoral responsiveness, which is not the suspected defect in this phagocytic presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The TREC screen detects severe T-cell lymphopenia (SCID) at birth; it does not identify a phagocytic killing defect.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 10-month-old boy has had recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections. Workup reveals absent B cells and markedly low serum immunoglobulins, and X-linked agammaglobulinemia is diagnosed. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term treatment?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vaccination with all available live vaccines

explanation.summary: Humoral inborn errors of immunity such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia are managed with immunoglobulin replacement.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that humoral IEIs lead to a loss of immunoglobulin, which can be replaced through intravenous or subcutaneous injection (IVIG or SCIG). Antibody deficiency is managed with immunoglobulin replacement with or without prophylactic antimicrobials.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematopoietic stem cell transplant is reserved for severe or combined immunodeficiencies (such as SCID or WAS), not for isolated antibody deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Many patients with humoral IEIs should not receive live vaccinations because they may be severely immunocompromised.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interferon-gamma is used as prophylaxis in phagocytic defects such as chronic granulomatous disease, not in antibody deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Discontinuing an immunosuppressant addresses a secondary immunodeficiency; this child has a primary humoral defect and is not on such a drug.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman takes several medications for rheumatoid arthritis and malignancy. Which of the following of her medications is least likely to cause a secondary immunodeficiency?

explanation.summary: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen inhibit cyclooxygenase but do not cause meaningful immunosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's review question makes clear that ibuprofen, an NSAID, inhibits the cyclooxygenase pathway but does not cause immune suppression, unlike the other listed drugs. Cancer chemotherapeutics, biologics, and corticosteroids all suppress immune cells or cytokines.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Methotrexate is a cytostatic immunosuppressant that decreases T- and B-cell proliferation and antibody responses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids such as cortisone decrease cytokines, phagocytosis, and chemotaxis, causing secondary immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A B-cell-depleting monoclonal antibody (for example, anti-CD20 rituximab) induces loss of B cells and predisposes to infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cancer chemotherapeutics such as adriamycin suppress the bone marrow and impair immune cell production.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with long-standing, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with recurrent bacterial skin infections. Which of the following best explains his increased susceptibility to infection?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A germline mutation causing absent B cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thymic aplasia with absent T cells

explanation.summary: Type 2 diabetes is a common medical cause of secondary immunodeficiency because hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil function.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists type 2 diabetes mellitus as one of the more common chronic medical causes of secondary immunodeficiency in adults, noting that hyperglycemia affects neutrophil function and cytokine production. This predisposes to recurrent bacterial infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Absent B cells from a germline defect describes a primary humoral IEI, not the acquired mechanism operating in diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A late complement deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria infection and is a primary immune defect, not a consequence of diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thymic aplasia (as in DiGeorge syndrome) is a congenital T-cell disorder unrelated to acquired diabetic immune impairment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autosplenectomy is characteristic of sickle cell disease; diabetes impairs immunity chiefly through neutrophil dysfunction.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever, productive cough, and chills. A chest x-ray documents pneumonia, the second such episode in 12 months. He is sexually active with multiple male partners and takes no medications. A complete blood count with differential shows lymphopenia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Refer immediately for hematopoietic stem cell transplant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Order a neutrophil oxidative burst assay

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reassure him that two pneumonias in a year is normal

explanation.summary: In an adult with recurrent infection, lymphopenia, and HIV risk factors, secondary immunodeficiency from HIV should be evaluated first.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that adults are more likely to have a secondary immunodeficiency than an IEI, so evaluation should focus on secondary causes. This patient has an HIV risk factor, and the brick's case concludes he should be tested for HIV and treated if infected; lymphopenia further supports this.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunoglobulin replacement treats humoral IEIs; it is premature and inappropriate before identifying a likely secondary cause such as HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematopoietic stem cell transplant is reserved for severe or combined primary immunodeficiencies, not for a suspected secondary cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The oxidative burst assay evaluates phagocytic defects (catalase-positive abscesses), which do not match this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two documented pneumonias in a year is a warning sign of immunodeficiency, so reassurance without evaluation is inappropriate.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child recovers from measles but over the following months develops several new bacterial and viral infections despite having previously been healthy. Which of the following best explains this transient increase in susceptibility?

explanation.summary: Measles can cause immunosuppression for months after the initial infection through loss of memory B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that measles can cause immunosuppression months after the initial infection due to T- and B-cell dysfunction, especially loss of memory B cells. This erases prior immunologic memory and increases susceptibility to infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A complement deficiency is a lifelong primary defect predisposing to Neisseria infection, not a transient post-measles susceptibility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Asplenia is not a described consequence of measles; it predisposes to encapsulated organisms in conditions such as sickle cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Diabetes-related immune impairment is unrelated to a recent measles infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An ADA defect causes SCID, a congenital combined immunodeficiency present from birth, not a transient post-viral state.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 5-month-old infant is diagnosed with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) after an abnormal newborn TREC screen. Which of the following interventions is contraindicated in this infant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administration of a live attenuated vaccine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evaluation for hematopoietic stem cell transplant

explanation.summary: Live vaccines are contraindicated in severely immunocompromised patients, especially those with combined B- and T-cell defects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that live virus vaccines are contraindicated in patients who are severely immunocompromised, especially those with B- and T-cell defects. An infant with SCID has a severe combined defect and could develop disseminated infection from a live vaccine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Prophylactic antimicrobials are appropriate supportive care to prevent infection in a severely immunodeficient infant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematopoietic stem cell transplant is the definitive treatment for combined immunodeficiencies such as SCID.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunoglobulin replacement is appropriate to compensate for absent antibody production while awaiting definitive therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protecting the infant from sick contacts is a reasonable measure to reduce infection risk, not a contraindicated intervention.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man taking a chronic immunosuppressant after a solid-organ transplant develops recurrent infections, and evaluation attributes this to a secondary immunodeficiency from his medication. Assuming it is clinically safe, which of the following is the most appropriate management approach?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Proceed to hematopoietic stem cell transplant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start lifelong immunoglobulin replacement regardless of levels

explanation.summary: Secondary immunodeficiency is managed by addressing the underlying cause, which for a drug-induced case means discontinuing or modifying the offending agent.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that management of secondary immunodeficiency usually requires addressing the underlying cause; if the patient is taking an immunosuppressant, treatment should be discontinued or modified if possible. Removing or reducing the causative drug directly reverses the immune impairment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Interferon-gamma prophylaxis is used for phagocytic defects such as CGD, not for drug-induced secondary immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematopoietic stem cell transplant treats severe primary combined immunodeficiencies, not a reversible drug effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Live vaccines are contraindicated in immunocompromised patients and would not address the underlying medication cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immunoglobulin replacement is directed at antibody deficiency; the first step here is to modify the causative immunosuppressant.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with no significant medical history is hospitalized with osteomyelitis of the tibia, and bone cultures grow Salmonella species. His physician states that this infection should prompt consideration of an immunodeficiency evaluation. Which of the following characteristics of this infection best justifies that concern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A common organism causing infection in an unusual location

choices.label: B
choices.text: A poor response to antimicrobial treatment

choices.label: C
choices.text: An infection meeting the frequency threshold for recurrence

choices.label: D
choices.text: An infection caused by an opportunistic organism

choices.label: E
choices.text: A persistent infection accompanied by weight change

explanation.summary: Salmonella osteomyelitis is the brick's example of an unusual infection: a common organism in an unusual location.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the hallmark characteristics of infection that raise concern for immunodeficiency, the brick defines 'unusual' infections as those with non-tuberculous mycobacteria, opportunistic infections, or common infections in unusual locations, giving Salmonella osteomyelitis as the specific example. Salmonella is a common pathogen, but bone is an unusual site, which is what makes this infection a warning sign.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Poor response to treatment refers to needing intravenous antibiotics, at least 8 weeks on antibiotics without improvement, multiple hospitalizations, or surgery to resolve an infection; nothing in the stem indicates treatment failure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recurrent infection requires frequency thresholds such as at least 4 bacterial infections or 2 pneumonias per year; this is a single episode.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Salmonella is a common organism, not an opportunist; the brick's opportunistic examples are Cryptosporidia and Pneumocystis jirovecii.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Persistent infections in the brick are chronic diarrhea with weight changes, persistent thrush, or persistent skin fungal infection, none of which is described here.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought to clinic by her parents, who are concerned about how often she gets sick. Which of the following elements of her history most clearly meets a threshold that should prompt evaluation for immunodeficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Three new ear infections in the past year

choices.label: B
choices.text: One serious sinus infection in the past year

choices.label: C
choices.text: Three confirmed bacterial infections in the past year

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nine weeks on antibiotics with no improvement

choices.label: E
choices.text: One episode of pneumonia in the past year

explanation.summary: Eight or more weeks on antibiotics without improvement is a poor-response-to-treatment warning sign; the other counts fall below the recurrent-infection thresholds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists poor response to treatment as a warning sign of immunodeficiency, specifically including at least 8 weeks on antibiotics without improvement. Nine weeks of antibiotics without improvement exceeds that threshold. Each of the other options falls just short of the numeric thresholds the brick sets for recurrent infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The recurrent-infection threshold is at least 4 new ear infections in a year; three does not meet it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The threshold is at least 2 serious sinus infections in a year; one does not meet it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The threshold is at least 4 confirmed bacterial infections per year; three does not meet it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The threshold is at least 2 pneumonias per year; a single pneumonia does not meet it.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy has had persistent oral thrush, chronic diarrhea with poor weight gain, and two episodes of pneumonia with encapsulated bacteria. On examination, tonsils are not visible and no lymph nodes are palpable. A CBC with differential, HIV antigen screen, and serum immunoglobulin levels are ordered. Which of the following additional studies is most appropriate for the immune defect suggested by this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lymphocyte mitogen and antigen stimulation assays

choices.label: B
choices.text: CH50 and AH50 total complement activity assays

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemoglobin A1c to screen for diabetes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chest CT to evaluate for an underlying thymoma

explanation.summary: Encapsulated and opportunistic infections, failure to thrive, and absent lymphoid tissue in a child point to a humoral and cell-mediated defect, whose workup includes lymphocyte mitogen and antigen stimulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pediatric evaluation schema groups recurrent infection with encapsulated organisms, opportunistic infections, failure to thrive, and lack of lymph node tissue as features that should raise suspicion for humoral and cell-mediated defects. The diagnostic evaluation for that branch includes serum immunoglobulins, IgG vaccine titers, serum albumin, B- and T-cell subsets, lymphocyte mitogen and antigen stimulations, and genetic testing as indicated. Lack of visible tonsils and palpable nodes is a physical finding the brick specifically directs clinicians to look for.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CH50 and AH50 are the workup for recurrent or severe Neisseria infection, which points to a complement defect rather than the combined defect suggested here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The oxidative burst assay evaluates phagocytic defects, which present with catalase-positive abscesses or infection with albinism and neurologic deficits.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin A1c is a diabetes screen listed for adult evaluation; diabetes is not a plausible cause of thrush, diarrhea, and absent lymphoid tissue in an infant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chest imaging for thymoma is considered in adults in whom this hematologic neoplasia is suspected, not in an infant with a likely inborn error of immunity.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has had two episodes of disseminated infection with non-tuberculous mycobacteria. His neutrophil oxidative burst assay and serum immunoglobulin levels are normal. A defect in which of the following is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Recurrent non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection reflects Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD), a cell-mediated IEI caused by defective IL-12/IFN-γ signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists infection with non-tuberculous mycobacteria as an 'unusual' warning-sign infection and classifies IL-12/IFN-γ deficiency (MSMD) among the cell-mediated immunodeficiencies caused by defects in required cytokine signaling. Normal oxidative burst and immunoglobulins argue against phagocytic and humoral defects, leaving the IL-12/IFN-γ axis as the most likely defect.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-2Rγ chain deficiency causes X-linked SCID, a global T-cell defect that presents with broad opportunistic infections and failure to thrive, not isolated mycobacterial susceptibility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A defective oxidative burst causes chronic granulomatous disease with catalase-positive abscesses, and his oxidative burst assay is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Late complement deficiencies predispose to recurrent Neisseria infection, not mycobacterial disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Costimulatory pathway defects cause hyper IgM syndrome, a humoral and cell-mediated defect; his normal immunoglobulin levels do not fit.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with recurrent sinopulmonary infections is diagnosed with hyper IgM syndrome. The underlying defect in this inborn error of immunity most directly involves which of the following?

explanation.summary: Hyper IgM syndrome is a combined humoral and cell-mediated IEI caused by a defect in costimulatory pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick classifies hyper IgM syndrome among the humoral and cell-mediated immunodeficiencies and attributes it specifically to defects in costimulatory pathways. This distinguishes it from the other combined defects in the same category, which arise from enzyme defects, cytoskeletal defects, apoptosis, or DNA repair and replication.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytoskeletal mechanism defects underlie Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thymic defects cause the cell-mediated immunodeficiency of DiGeorge syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defects in enzymes critical to lymphocyte development cause ADA-SCID and RAG-SCID.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Required cytokine signaling defects cause IL-2Rγ chain deficiency (X-linked SCID) and IL-12/IFN-γ deficiency (MSMD).

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl with albinism and neurologic deficits has had recurrent skin abscesses and lymphadenitis. After a CBC with differential, which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic evaluation for the immune defect suggested by this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neutrophil oxidative burst assay and peripheral blood smear

choices.label: B
choices.text: CH50, AH50, C3, and C4 complement levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum immunoglobulin levels and specific vaccine titers

choices.label: D
choices.text: B- and T-cell subset counts and mitogen stimulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum albumin, total protein, and IgE levels

explanation.summary: Recurrent infection with albinism and neurologic deficits points to a phagocytic defect (Chédiak-Higashi syndrome), evaluated with the oxidative burst assay and peripheral blood smear.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pediatric evaluation schema lists recurrent infection with albinism and neurologic deficits, together with skin or liver abscesses and lymphadenitis, as findings that should prompt suspicion of a phagocytic defect. The diagnostic evaluation for that branch is the neutrophil oxidative burst, a peripheral blood smear, and genetic testing as indicated. Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is one of the innate immunodeficiencies the brick lists.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement assays are indicated for recurrent or severe Neisseria infection, not for abscesses with albinism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunoglobulin levels and vaccine titers belong to the humoral and cell-mediated branch, prompted by encapsulated or opportunistic infections and failure to thrive.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymphocyte subsets and mitogen stimulation also belong to the humoral and cell-mediated branch, not the phagocytic-defect workup.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum albumin and IgE are part of the humoral and cell-mediated evaluation; they do not assess phagocyte function.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: Which of the following disorders is classified as a complement immunodeficiency?

explanation.summary: Hereditary angioedema is grouped with the complement immunodeficiencies alongside early and late complement deficiencies and PNH.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's classification of inborn errors of immunity lists complement immunodeficiencies as early complement deficiencies, late (MAC) complement deficiencies, hereditary angioedema (HAE), and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). The other options belong to different categories of IEI.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency I is classified as an innate immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is classified as an innate immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myeloperoxidase deficiency is classified as an innate immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMCC) is listed under cell-mediated immunodeficiencies (central tolerance) and pattern-recognition receptor immunodeficiencies.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has had recurrent bacterial pneumonia and one year of chronic diarrhea with peripheral edema. Laboratory studies show low serum IgG, low serum albumin, and lymphopenia with a decreased CD4+ T-cell count. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his laboratory findings?

explanation.summary: Protein-losing enteropathy causes hypogammaglobulinemia and CD4+ lymphopenia and must be excluded before diagnosing an inborn error of immunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists protein-losing enteropathy as a medical cause of secondary immunodeficiency that leads to hypogammaglobulinemia (low IgG) and lymphopenia, especially of CD4+ T cells. The pediatric schema directs clinicians to rule out GI or renal loss of immunoglobulin (which is why serum albumin is part of the workup) before attributing low immunoglobulins to an IEI. Chronic diarrhea, edema, and low albumin together with low IgG and CD4+ lymphopenia fit GI protein loss.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Common variable immunodeficiency is a humoral IEI that would not explain the low albumin, edema, and CD4+ lymphopenia produced by GI protein loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: X-linked agammaglobulinemia is a humoral IEI with absent B cells and very low immunoglobulins; it does not cause hypoalbuminemia or selective CD4+ loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Selective IgA deficiency lowers IgA only and does not account for low IgG, low albumin, or lymphopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronic granulomatous disease is a phagocytic defect causing catalase-positive abscesses with normal immunoglobulins and lymphocyte counts.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has had multiple episodes of pneumonia requiring intravenous antibiotics. Which of the following best explains her increased susceptibility to infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disruption of the normal mucosal barrier

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of immunoglobulins through the kidney

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bone marrow invasion impairing immune cell production

explanation.summary: Cystic fibrosis causes secondary immunodeficiency by disrupting the normal mucosal barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among chronic medical conditions that cause secondary immunodeficiency, the brick states that cystic fibrosis disrupts the normal mucosal barrier. This loss of barrier defense, rather than a defect in immune cells or proteins, underlies her recurrent respiratory infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of immunoglobulins is the mechanism the brick attributes to chronic kidney disease, not cystic fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperglycemia impairing neutrophil function is the mechanism in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bone marrow invasion is how hematologic neoplasia such as multiple myeloma causes immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Asplenia is the mechanism in sickle cell disease, not cystic fibrosis.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has had three episodes of bacterial pneumonia in the past 18 months. He takes no medications, an HIV screen is negative, and hemoglobin A1c is normal. Serum IgG, IgA, and IgM are all low. Which of the following is most appropriate to evaluate for a neoplastic secondary cause of his immunodeficiency?

explanation.summary: In an adult with hypogammaglobulinemia and no other secondary cause, chest imaging is used to evaluate for thymoma with immunodeficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists hematologic neoplasia, including multiple myeloma and thymoma with immunodeficiency, among the medical causes of secondary immunodeficiency in adults. In its adult diagnostic studies, it states that a chest CT or x-ray may be considered if thymoma is suspected, with further evaluation if a malignancy is suspected. This older adult with acquired hypogammaglobulinemia and no medication, infectious, or metabolic explanation warrants that imaging.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The oxidative burst assay evaluates phagocytic defects such as CGD, which do not cause hypogammaglobulinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complement assays are indicated for recurrent Neisseria infection and do not identify a neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymphocyte mitogen stimulation assesses lymphocyte function in suspected IEI; it does not detect a thymoma or other neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The neonatal TREC screen identifies severe T-cell lymphopenia at birth and is part of the pediatric evaluation, not an adult neoplasm workup.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is hospitalized with his second episode of Streptococcus pneumoniae septicemia. Which of the following best explains his increased susceptibility to this infection?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of immunoglobulins through the kidney

explanation.summary: Sickle cell disease causes secondary immunodeficiency through asplenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists sickle cell disease leading to asplenia among the medical conditions that cause secondary immunodeficiency. Two episodes of septicemia is also a 'severe' warning sign of immunodeficiency, and here the underlying explanation is the loss of splenic function that accompanies sickle cell disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Renal loss of immunoglobulins is the mechanism of chronic kidney disease, not sickle cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Impaired granuloma formation is the effect of TNF-α inhibitor therapy, which this child is not receiving.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of memory B cells is the mechanism of post-measles immunosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A defective oxidative burst causes chronic granulomatous disease, an inborn error of immunity unrelated to sickle cell disease.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with trisomy 21 has had recurrent respiratory infections. Which of the following best categorizes her immunodeficiency?

explanation.summary: Chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 21 and Turner syndrome are classified as medical causes of secondary immunodeficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 21 and monosomy XO (Turner syndrome) among the medical disorders that cause secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency, alongside diabetes, protein-losing enteropathy, chronic kidney and liver disease, cystic fibrosis, hematologic neoplasia, and sickle cell disease. Although present from birth, these are not categorized as inborn errors of immunity in the brick's scheme.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Humoral IEIs are selective IgA deficiency, CVID, and X-linked agammaglobulinemia, not chromosomal syndromes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cell-mediated IEIs include DiGeorge syndrome, CMCC, X-linked SCID, and MSMD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Innate IEIs are CGD, LAD I, Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, and myeloperoxidase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Complement IEIs are early and late complement deficiencies, HAE, and PNH.

questions.topicName: Diagnosis and Treatment of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV infection is evaluated in clinic. Which of the following findings would be most indicative of a CD4+ T-cell count below 200 cells/mm³?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma at sites of sexual contact
